title: The replication crisis
hook: in 2015 only about 36 percent of a hundred psychology studies replicated clearly (Open Science Collaboration)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the section on compassion with a farmer who tugged his grain. Your line was it grows: tended, slowly, without force.

A hundred psychology studies, already published in respected journals, were run a second time. Same questions, same methods, as close as the new teams could get, often with help from the original authors. Nearly all the originals had reported a clear result. The repeats? About 36 percent did. That came from a large group of researchers calling themselves the Open Science Collaboration. This path has spent weeks sharing findings from labs, so it owes you this part too. A new section starts today: the honest part.
screen: `A HUNDRED STUDIES, RUN AGAIN.` → `ABOUT 36 PERCENT HELD CLEARLY.` → `THE HONEST PART BEGINS.`

segments.voice: First, what was done. The point wasn't to catch anyone out. It was a plain question: if you do the same study again, do you get the same answer? The teams repeated each study once, carefully, and published everything, including the misses. Second, what came back. Only about a third of the repeats showed a clear result, and where an effect did show up again, it was often smaller than first reported. Third, what that does and doesn't mean. A failed repeat doesn't prove the original was wrong, and it certainly doesn't prove anyone cheated. A single repeat can miss too. What it means is humbler: one study is a first word, not a last word. A finding earns trust by surviving being done again, by other people, in other places. Fourth, an old line that already knew this. The book of Proverbs, in the King James text, says: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him." The first account tends to sound right. Then the neighbor arrives and checks. Replication is the neighbor. And it applies here: many findings this path has shared were single studies, and a few came with a note that later work was mixed. That's no reason to throw them out. It's a reason to hold them like any first account: with interest, and a question ready.
screen: `ASK THE SAME QUESTION TWICE.` · `ABOUT A THIRD HELD UP CLEARLY.` · `ONE STUDY IS A FIRST WORD.` · `THE NEIGHBOR COMES TO CHECK.` · then, large: `WAS IT REPEATED?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one finding you've taken on board, from this path, a headline or a friend: phones make us dumber, gratitude makes us happier, whatever comes. Hold it for a few breaths and ask quietly: was it repeated? If you don't know, let the not-knowing sit beside the finding without pushing either one away.
The replication crisis. When psychology repeated its own studies, many results came back weaker or didn't come back at all. Today's word.
Your line: was it repeated? It's a kind question, not a cynical one. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Researchers check a finding by running the same study again, often with new teams and larger groups; a result that holds up across repeats is trusted more than a single striking study.

chat.says: I read most psychology studies failed when redone. So it's all fake, right?
options: No. A failed repeat isn't proof of fraud; one study is a first word, not the last.
Pretty much. When a study fails to repeat, it shows the first team cheated.
No. The repeats failed because the new teams changed all the methods on purpose.

notes: Confirm the Open Science Collaboration figures as stated: 100 studies from three psychology journals; about 97 percent of originals reported significant results; about 36 percent of replications did; replication effect sizes were on average smaller (roughly half). The voice says 'nearly all', 'about 36 percent', 'about a third' and 'often smaller'.
'Often with help from the original authors': the project contacted original authors for materials and review of protocols; confirm the phrasing.

The KJV keeps 'neighbour' inside the quotation.
